title: Rehat as love
hookLine: rules kept from love, not fear

lines: ONE HAS A TIMER IN THE DOORWAY.
ONE CAN'T GET THE TUNE OUT OF HER HEAD.
cards: Every evening, in one house, a teenager practices a piano piece because a parent is standing in the doorway with a timer.
In the house next door, another teenager practices the same piece because she heard it once on a rainy afternoon and can't get it out of her head.
From the hallway, they sound almost the same: same scales, same wrong notes, same hour. Ask each of them in ten years whether they still play, and you'll likely hear two very different answers.
A code can be kept the first way. Did the Gurus mean it to be kept the second?

teach.b: Begin with the Japji, at its twenty-first step, on Ang 4. Guru Nanak names three things together: hearing, believing, and holding love in the mind.
In paraphrase, the one who hears, accepts and loves bathes at a shrine deep inside. The order matters. Hearing comes first, and love is where it lands.
Then a line from Guru Nanak on Ang 1412, in paraphrase: if you want to play the game of love, come to my lane with your head on your palm. That's not a soft line. It asks for everything.
But it calls the asking a game of love, not a duty roster. Now, honestly: the Gurus also speak of bhau, a word for fear, or awe, of God, and the Japji itself talks about it.
Some readers hear awe in it more than terror, the feeling of standing before something vast. Love and awe sit side by side in the hymns, without one canceling the other.
But it's love the Gurus call a game, and love they ask to be played. So read the rehat that way.

teach.h: THE SAME RULE, KEPT TWO WAYS.
teach.b: The kesh, the morning banis, the clear mind, faithfulness at home: they can be kept with someone standing in the doorway, a parent, a community, a worry about what people will say.
Or they can be kept the way the second student plays, because the tune is already inside. The code itself can't tell the difference from the hallway. Only the one keeping it knows.

how: Some Sikh teachers describe the rehat as a way of loving the Guru, and point to Guru Nanak's line on Ang 1412 about playing the game of love.

o: a rule that Sikhs may marry only for love
the love songs sung at a Sikh wedding
keeping the code from love, not only from fear

games.q: inside rehat as love: tap the pairs.
p: the game of love, head on your palm
plays because the tune is inside

s: the Gurus never speak of fear of God
they speak of bhau, which some readers hear as awe, and it sits beside love in the hymns.
Guru Nanak calls the path a game of love
on Ang 1412: come to my lane with your head on your palm, if you want to play the game of love.
from the outside you can always tell why someone keeps a rule
like the two students in the hallway, the same practice can be kept from fear or from love.

games.q: in the Japji's twenty-first step, Guru Nanak names three things. where does love come?
games.why: hearing, believing, and then love held in the mind: the inner bath at the shrine within.

practice: Bring to mind one rule you already keep, a habit, a promise, a line you won't cross, and ask gently why you keep it: is someone standing in the doorway, or is there a tune you love underneath? There's no wrong answer.
Then hold that rule as something you'd choose again today, and let the breath be easy.

wordCard.voice: Rehat as love. The Gurus put love at the end of hearing and believing, and call the whole path a game of love. The rules can be kept from fear or from love; the hymns point to love. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: love, loving devotion. in the Japji it comes after hearing and believing.

carryVoice: Your line: kept in love. The same rule, kept from the inside out. Rest well.

sources.ref: Ang 1412 (Salok Varan te Vadhik, Guru Nanak)
